skillCheck.title: Run, Read, and Repair JavaScript Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: Nia wants to run the same welcome message tomorrow without retyping its JavaScript. Which approach best fits that goal?

options.label: Enter the statements in the Node REPL and close it when the result appears
Save the statements in `welcome.js` and run `node welcome.js` when needed
Type the message directly in PowerShell and leave the terminal window open
Keep the statements in an unsaved VS Code tab and reopen VS Code tomorrow

questions.explanation: A saved `.js` file preserves the source and can be run again with Node. The REPL is useful for temporary experiments, but its entered statements are not a repeatable program file.

questions.prompt: Omar changes the greeting in `hello.js`, but rerunning the file still shows the old greeting. What should he check first?

options.label: Whether the terminal text was selected before the command ran
Whether the JavaScript file was renamed after the first run
Whether the Node REPL contains a copy of the new greeting
Whether `hello.js` was saved before he reran the Node command

questions.explanation: Node reads the saved contents of the source file when the command runs. An unsaved editor change is not yet part of the file that Node executes.

questions.prompt: PowerShell is at `C:\Users\Maya`, while `hello.js` is inside `C:\Users\Maya\week-01`. Which command sequence runs that file from its folder?

options.label: `cd ./week-01` followed by `node ./hello.js`
`node ./week-01` followed by `cd ./hello.js`
`cd ./hello.js` followed by `node ./week-01`
`node cd ./week-01` followed by `./hello.js`

questions.explanation: `cd ./week-01` changes the current folder to the one containing the source file. From there, `node ./hello.js` asks Node to execute that file.

questions.prompt: A learner runs `node hello.js` and sees `Cannot find module C:\Users\Tara\hello.js`. VS Code shows the file at `C:\Users\Tara\practice\hello.js`. What does the error most strongly indicate?

options.label: The `.js` extension prevents Node from reading the source file
The program must be entered in the REPL before Node can run it
The terminal is looking in the parent folder instead of `practice`
The source file must be moved into the Node installation folder

questions.explanation: The path in the error shows exactly where Node looked. Because the real file is one folder deeper, the learner should enter `practice` or supply the correct path before rerunning the command.

questions.prompt: VS Code displays and edits `welcome.js`, while Node executes its statements. Which description assigns those roles correctly?

options.label: VS Code is the runtime, and Node is the project folder
VS Code is the editor, and Node is the runtime
VS Code is the terminal, and Node is the source file
VS Code is the source file, and Node is the editor

questions.explanation: The editor is where the learner changes the source text. The Node runtime reads and executes the saved JavaScript when invoked from the terminal.

questions.prompt: A script must display `Welcome, Ada!` in the terminal when Node runs it. Which statement produces that visible output?

options.label: `console.log("Welcome, Ada!");`
`"Welcome, Ada!";`
`node("Welcome, Ada!");`
`console = "Welcome, Ada!";`

questions.explanation: `console.log(...)` sends its argument to the terminal output. A string expression by itself is not printed when it appears in a script run by Node.

questions.prompt: Entering `2 + 3` in the Node REPL shows `5`, but a file containing only `2 + 3;` shows nothing when run. Why are the results presented differently?

options.label: The REPL converts arithmetic into text, while scripts keep it numeric
The REPL saves every expression, while scripts delete unused expressions
The REPL uses a different addition operator from a JavaScript file
The REPL echoes expression results, while a script needs an output statement

questions.explanation: The REPL is interactive, so it echoes the value of an entered expression. During normal script execution, an expression can run without being displayed; `console.log` makes the value visible.

questions.prompt: The Node REPL shows `test` and then `undefined` after `console.log("test")`. What does the second line represent?

options.label: A warning that the string was not stored in a file
An error caused by calling `console.log` inside the REPL
The return value of `console.log` after it printed the string
A placeholder for text that Node failed to print to the terminal

questions.explanation: `console.log` first prints `test`. The REPL then echoes the call's return value, which is `undefined`; that second line does not mean the print failed.

questions.prompt: The terminal currently shows the Node REPL prompt `>`. Which entered command returns to the normal PowerShell prompt?

options.label: `.exit`
`.save`
`node.exit`
`exit.node`

questions.explanation: `.exit` is the assigned REPL command for ending the interactive session. After it runs, the terminal returns to PowerShell, where normal shell commands can be used again.

questions.prompt: In the command `node welcome.js`, what do the two parts tell the computer to do?

options.label: `node` names the folder, and `welcome.js` selects the terminal
`node` creates the source, and `welcome.js` opens the editor
`node` names the output, and `welcome.js` installs the runtime
`node` starts the runtime, and `welcome.js` names the source to execute

questions.explanation: `node` invokes the JavaScript runtime. `welcome.js` is the file argument that tells the runtime which saved source program to execute.

skillCheck.title: Values, Variables, and Predictable Calculations Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: A program stores a tax rate that must remain the same for the entire run. Which declaration communicates that intention?

options.label: `let taxRate;`
`let taxRate = 0.075;`
`const taxRate = 0.075;`
`taxRate const = 0.075;`

questions.explanation: `const` creates a binding that cannot be reassigned and requires its initial value immediately. That matches a tax rate intended to remain unchanged during this run.

questions.prompt: A running total starts at zero and changes whenever an expense is added. Which declaration fits that behavior?

options.label: `let total = 0;`
`const total = 0;`
`total let = 0;`
`const total;`

questions.explanation: `let` is appropriate when the binding will be deliberately reassigned. A running total changes, whereas a `const` binding cannot be assigned a new number later.

questions.prompt: A room-selection variable is deliberately empty: `const selectedRoom = null;`. What does `typeof selectedRoom` produce, and what should the learner conclude?

options.label: `"null"`; JavaScript reports null as its own typeof category.
`"undefined"`; null and an unassigned binding are identical values.
`"object"`; selectedRoom can therefore be used as an ordinary record object.
`"object"`; this is a historical typeof quirk, while the value itself is still null.

questions.explanation: `typeof null` returns `"object"` because of a historical JavaScript quirk. The value is still null, not an ordinary record whose properties can safely be read, and it is distinct from undefined.

questions.prompt: Consider `const fee = 500; fee = 600;`. What happens when JavaScript reaches the second statement?

options.label: The binding changes to 600 because both values are numbers
A reassignment error occurs because `fee` was declared with `const`
A second binding named `fee` is created with the new value
The second statement is ignored and execution always continues silently

questions.explanation: `const` prevents reassignment of the binding. JavaScript therefore raises an error at `fee = 600` instead of silently changing or duplicating the binding.

questions.prompt: Given `const remaining = 8500;`, which statement prints `Remaining: 8500` by interpolating the value?

options.label: `console.log("Remaining: ${remaining}");`
`console.log("Remaining: " - remaining);`
``console.log(`Remaining: ${remaining}`);``
`console.log(remaining = "Remaining: ");`

questions.explanation: A template literal uses backticks around the text and `${expression}` for interpolation. Ordinary quotes would print the placeholder characters rather than evaluate `remaining`.

questions.prompt: A learner writes `let roomNumber;` and checks `typeof roomNumber` before assigning anything. Which result should they expect?

options.label: `"number"`, because the name contains the word Number
`"undefined"`, because no value has been assigned yet
`"string"`, because every variable name is text
`"boolean"`, because the room either exists or does not

questions.explanation: A declared `let` binding without an assigned value currently contains `undefined`. The identifier's spelling does not determine the type of the value it holds.

questions.prompt: What value is assigned by `const result = "12" + 3;`?

options.label: The string `"123"`
The number `15`
The string `"15"`
The number `123`

questions.explanation: When one operand of `+` is a string, JavaScript concatenates here, producing the string `"123"`. Numeric addition requires converting the text first.

questions.prompt: A budget program receives `rawCost` as the string `"12"`. Which expression produces the number `15` after adding 3?

options.label: `rawCost + 3`
`String(rawCost) + 3`
`typeof rawCost + 3`
`Number(rawCost) + 3`

questions.explanation: `Number(rawCost)` converts the numeric text to the number `12` before addition, so the result is the number `15`. Leaving it as text would concatenate instead.

questions.prompt: Without adding parentheses, what does `2 + 3 * 4` evaluate to?

options.label: `20`, because addition always runs before multiplication
`14`, because multiplication runs before addition
`24`, because all three numbers are multiplied
`9`, because operations run strictly from left to right

questions.explanation: Multiplication has higher precedence than addition, so JavaScript calculates `3 * 4` first and then adds `2`, giving `14`.

questions.prompt: Seventeen lab seats are arranged in rows of five. Which value does `17 % 5` produce for the seats left over?
questions.explanation: The remainder operator `%` reports what remains after whole groups are removed. Three full groups of five use 15 seats, leaving 2.

skillCheck.title: Decisions and Input Validation Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: Why does `"5" === 5` evaluate to `false`?

options.label: Strict equality can compare only two strings at a time
Strict equality treats every numeric string as zero
Strict equality compares the variable names instead of their values
Strict equality requires both the value and the type to match

questions.explanation: The left value is a string and the right value is a number. Strict equality does not coerce them to the same type, so they do not match.

questions.prompt: Given `const absences = 0;`, what is the result of `absences !== 0`?

options.label: `true`, because `!==` always reverses a numeric value
`false`, because both sides are the same number value and type
`0`, because an inequality expression returns one of its operands
`undefined`, because zero cannot be used in a strict comparison

questions.explanation: Both operands are the number `0`, so they are strictly equal. The strict-inequality expression therefore evaluates to the boolean `false`.

questions.prompt: A booking accepts groups of at least 12 people. For `const groupSize = 12;`, which condition correctly includes that boundary?

options.label: `groupSize > 12`
`groupSize === "12"`
`groupSize >= 12`
`groupSize !== 12`

questions.explanation: “At least 12” includes 12 itself and every larger value, which is exactly what `>= 12` expresses. A plain `>` would reject the boundary.

questions.prompt: A program uses `if (attendance >= 75) { console.log("Eligible"); } else { console.log("Review"); }`. What prints when `attendance` is 80?

options.label: `Eligible`
`Review`
Both messages
Neither message

questions.explanation: `80 >= 75` is true, so JavaScript runs the `if` block and skips the paired `else` block. Only `Eligible` is printed.

questions.prompt: A score of 92 is checked by `if (score >= 50)`, followed by `else if (score >= 80)`. Which outcome follows from that order?

options.label: Neither branch runs because both conditions are true
Both branches run because 92 satisfies both conditions
Only the `>= 80` branch runs because it is more specific
Only the `>= 50` branch runs because it is the first true branch

questions.explanation: An `if`/`else if` chain stops at its first true condition. The broad `>= 50` check matches first, so the later `>= 80` branch is never reached; the more specific test should come first if it needs distinct behavior.

questions.prompt: Event entry requires a valid ticket and an age of at least 18. Which condition enforces both requirements?

options.label: `hasValidTicket && age >= 18`
`hasValidTicket || age >= 18`
`!hasValidTicket && age >= 18`
`hasValidTicket === age >= 18`

questions.explanation: `&&` is true only when both operands are true, matching a rule that requires the ticket check and the age check. `||` would admit someone who meets only one requirement.

questions.prompt: A lab permits entry when a person is a student or a staff member. Which expression matches that rule?

options.label: `isStudent && isStaff`
`!isStudent || !isStaff`
`isStudent || isStaff`
`isStudent === isStaff`

questions.explanation: `||` accepts the case where either role is true, including when both are true. `&&` would incorrectly require one person to hold both roles.

questions.prompt: If `isClosed` is `false`, what does `!isClosed` evaluate to?

options.label: `false`, because `!` preserves a boolean value
`true`, because `!` negates the boolean value
`undefined`, because `!` applies only to numbers
`0`, because false becomes a numeric result

questions.explanation: Logical NOT reverses a boolean value. Negating `false` produces `true`, which can express a condition such as “the venue is not closed.”

questions.prompt: A program runs `const amount = Number("desk");`. What does `Number.isFinite(amount)` return?

options.label: `true`, because `Number()` always creates a usable number
`"desk"`, because the original text is preserved as the result
`NaN`, because `Number.isFinite` returns the value it checks
`false`, because the failed conversion is not a finite number

questions.explanation: `Number("desk")` produces `NaN`, which is not a finite number. `Number.isFinite` returns the boolean `false`, allowing the program to take its invalid-input branch.

questions.prompt: A check-in program receives age as text and accepts ages from 16 through 120. Which sequence separates invalid text from an out-of-range number?

options.label: Convert with `Number`, reject when not finite, then check the lower and upper bounds
Check the text bounds first, convert with `String`, then call `Number.isFinite`
Call `Number.isFinite` on the original text, then compare the text with both bounds
Compare only with 16, then convert with `Number` after the acceptance message

questions.explanation: The program first needs a numeric value. It can then reject a failed conversion with `Number.isFinite` before applying `age >= 16 && age <= 120`. JavaScript needs two comparisons joined with `&&`; mathematical chained-range notation does not enforce this rule.

skillCheck.title: Arrays, Loops, and Summaries Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: A course planner must keep five task names in their intended order and process them as one list. Which starting representation fits that requirement?

options.label: An array containing the five task-name strings
Five unrelated variables with one task in each
One number containing the total number of tasks
One Boolean that records whether any task exists

questions.explanation: An array models one ordered collection and gives the program a single value to inspect or loop through. Separate variables scatter the collection, while a count or Boolean loses the task names.

questions.prompt: Given `const stages = ["plan", "code", "test", "share"]`, which expression reads the final stage without hard-coding its index?

options.label: stages[stages.length]
stages[0]
stages[stages.length - 1]
stages.indexOf("share")

questions.explanation: Array indexes start at zero, so the last valid index is one less than `length`. `stages[stages.length]` is just beyond the array, index 0 is the first item, and `indexOf` returns an index rather than the item.

questions.prompt: The array `attendees` already contains the names registered so far. Which statement adds `"Nora"` to the end while preserving the existing names?

options.label: attendees.pop("Nora")
attendees.push("Nora")
attendees.indexOf("Nora")
attendees.length("Nora")

questions.explanation: `push` appends a value to the array. `pop` removes the final value, `indexOf` searches, and `length` is a numeric property rather than a method for adding items.

questions.prompt: `const rooms = ["Lab A", "Lab B"]` is followed by `const position = rooms.indexOf("Studio")`. What value is stored in `position`?

options.label: 0, because no matching item was found
2, because the array contains two items
undefined, because `indexOf` has no return value
-1, because the requested value is absent

questions.explanation: `indexOf` returns the matching zero-based index, or `-1` when the value is not present. The array length and a valid first index do not signal absence.

questions.prompt: `const queue = ["Ada", "Bola", "Chen"]` is followed by `const removed = queue.pop()`. Which state is correct immediately afterward?

options.label: `removed` is `"Chen"`, and `queue` contains `"Ada"` and `"Bola"`
`removed` is `"Ada"`, and `queue` contains `"Bola"` and `"Chen"`
`removed` is `2`, and `queue` still contains all three names
`removed` is `undefined`, and `queue` becomes empty

questions.explanation: `pop()` removes and returns the last array item. It does not remove the first item, return the new length, or clear the whole array.

questions.prompt: A program needs to print every name in `attendees`, and it does not need each name’s index. Which loop expresses that intention most directly?

options.label: `while (attendees) { console.log(attendees); }`
`if (attendees.length > 0) { console.log(attendees); }`
`for (let i = attendees.length; i > 0; i++) { console.log(i); }`
`for (const name of attendees) { console.log(name); }`

questions.explanation: `for...of` supplies each array value directly. The `if` runs only once, the `while` condition never consumes the array, and the counted loop moves away from its stopping point while printing indexes rather than names.

questions.prompt: What indexes does this loop visit? `for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { console.log(i); }`
questions.explanation: The initializer gives 0 first, the condition permits values below 3, and `i++` increases by one after each iteration. The loop stops before 3.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? `const scores = [8, 6, 10]; let total = 0; for (const score of scores) { total = total + score; } console.log(total);`
questions.explanation: The accumulator begins at 0 and becomes 8, then 14, then 24 as the loop visits each numeric value. The code adds numbers, not indexes or text.

questions.prompt: A loop should print each item in `tasks` exactly once, but `for (let i = 0; i <= tasks.length; i++)` prints one extra `undefined`. Which change repairs the boundary?

options.label: Start with `i = 1` and keep `<=`
Replace `i++` with `i--`
Replace `tasks.length` with `tasks.length + 1`
Replace `i <= tasks.length` with `i < tasks.length`

questions.explanation: Valid indexes run from 0 through `length - 1`, so the loop must stop when `i` reaches `length`. Starting at 1 skips the first item, decrementing moves the wrong way, and adding one widens the error.

questions.prompt: A report must print labels such as `1. plan`, `2. code`, and `3. test` from an array. Why is a counted `for` loop a suitable choice?

options.label: It automatically sorts the array before every iteration
It provides an index that can be converted to the displayed position number
It prevents the array values from being read by the loop body
It runs only when the array contains exactly three items

questions.explanation: A counted loop exposes `i`, so the display can use `i + 1` while the code reads `array[i]`. It does not sort, hide values, or require a fixed array length.

skillCheck.title: Functions, Returns, and Scope Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: In `function formatMessage(name) { return `Hello, ${name}`; }`, followed by `formatMessage("Mira")`, which statement is accurate?

options.label: `"Mira"` is the parameter, and `name` is the argument
`name` is the parameter, and `"Mira"` is the argument
`formatMessage` is the argument, and `name` is the return value
`Hello` is the parameter, and `"Mira"` is the function declaration

questions.explanation: A parameter is the name in the function declaration; an argument is the value supplied by a particular call. Here `name` receives the argument `"Mira"` for that call.

questions.prompt: A function calculates a delivery fee that another calculation must use. Which function body provides that fee to its caller?

options.label: `const fee = amount * 0.1; return fee;`
`const fee = amount * 0.1; console.log(fee);`
`const fee = amount * 0.1; typeof fee;`
`const fee = amount * 0.1; String(fee);`

questions.explanation: `return fee` gives the calculated value back to the call expression, where other code can store or combine it. Logging only displays it, while `typeof` and `String` do not return anything here without an explicit `return`.

questions.prompt: What is stored in `result` after this code runs? `function double(value) { value * 2; } const result = double(6);`

options.label: The number 6
The number 12
The value undefined
The value null

questions.explanation: The multiplication expression is evaluated, but the function has no `return` statement, so the call produces `undefined`. JavaScript does not return the final expression automatically.

questions.prompt: Why does the final line fail? `function makeLabel() { const label = "Ready"; return label; } makeLabel(); console.log(label);`

options.label: The function must be called twice before its variables exist
A returned string cannot be printed with `console.log`
`const` variables may contain only numbers inside functions
`label` is local to the function and is not available outside its scope

questions.explanation: `label` is declared inside `makeLabel`, so its name exists only within that function body. Returning its value does not make the local variable itself globally available.

questions.prompt: A program calculates the same service fee in three branches. The rule will change next month. Which revision best reduces the chance of updating one branch but forgetting another?

options.label: Copy the calculation into a fourth branch as a backup
Move the rule into one named function and call it from each branch
Rename each branch variable so the copies look different
Print every intermediate value but keep all three copies

questions.explanation: One focused function gives the rule a single implementation point and lets all three branches reuse it. More copies or different names preserve the maintenance risk; logging may reveal values but does not remove duplication.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? `function addFee(amount, fee) { const total = amount + fee; return total; } const first = addFee(10, 2); const second = addFee(first, 3); console.log(second);`
questions.explanation: The first call returns 12. That returned value becomes the `amount` argument of the second call, which returns 15. Each call has its own local `total`.

questions.prompt: Why might `function calculateTotal(price, quantity)` use parameters instead of fixed numbers inside the function body?

options.label: The same calculation can run with different values supplied by each call
Parameters force every function call to produce text
Parameters make local variables visible throughout the whole program
The function can run without ever being called

questions.explanation: Parameters define the inputs a function needs, so callers can reuse the same behavior with different prices and quantities. They do not determine output type, widen scope, or call the function automatically.

questions.prompt: What does `status(72)` return? `function status(score) { if (score >= 50) { return "pass"; } return "retry"; }`

options.label: `"retry"`, because the final return always replaces the first
`undefined`, because the function contains two return statements
`"pass"`, because that return ends the call before the later line runs
`true`, because the condition is true

questions.explanation: For 72, the condition is true and the first `return` immediately finishes the function with `"pass"`. The later return is used only when the condition is false.

questions.prompt: What does this program print? `function announceReady() { console.log("Ready"); } console.log("Set");`

options.label: `Set` only, because declaring `announceReady` does not call it
`Ready` then `Set`, because every function declaration runs immediately
`Ready` only, because the function declaration replaces the later statement
Nothing, because a declared function prevents top-level statements from running

questions.explanation: A function declaration makes the function available but does not execute its body. Because `announceReady()` is never called, only the top-level `console.log("Set")` runs.

questions.prompt: Consider `const label = "outside"; function readLabel() { const label = "inside"; return label; } const result = readLabel();`. Which values are stored in `result` and the outer `label` afterward?

options.label: `result` is `"outside"`; outer `label` is `"inside"`
`result` is `undefined`; outer `label` is `"inside"`
`result` is `"inside"`; outer `label` is also `"inside"`
`result` is `"inside"`; outer `label` remains `"outside"`

questions.explanation: Inside the function, the local `label` is the name that gets returned. It is a separate binding, so the outer `label` remains unchanged after the call.

skillCheck.title: Objects, Classes, and JSON Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: A program needs one book record with a title, borrower, and returned status. Which value represents those related named fields most directly?

options.label: `["Orbit", "Mina", false]` with every meaning remembered by position
`"Orbit,Mina,false"` stored as one unparsed string
`{ title: "Orbit", borrower: "Mina", returned: false }`
`3`, representing the number of fields in the record

questions.explanation: An object associates each value with a descriptive property name, which matches a record made of named fields. The array and string contain the values but make their meanings depend on position or extra parsing; a count loses the data.

questions.prompt: Given `const field = "borrower"` and `const book = { title: "Orbit", borrower: "Mina" }`, which expression reads the property named by `field`?

options.label: `book.field` using dot notation
`book."borrower"` using a quoted name
`book(field)` using call syntax
`book[field]` using bracket notation

questions.explanation: Bracket notation evaluates `field` and uses its value, `"borrower"`, as the property key. `book.field` asks for a property literally named `field`, while the other forms are not property-access syntax.

questions.prompt: The object `book` currently has `returned: false`. Which statement updates that existing property to the Boolean value `true`?

options.label: `book.returned = true;` using assignment
`book.returned === true;` using comparison
`book[true] = "returned";` using a Boolean key
`book.returned(true);` using call syntax

questions.explanation: Assignment with `=` changes the property value. Strict equality only compares, the bracket statement targets a key named `"true"`, and a Boolean property is not a function to call.

questions.prompt: A program will create many book records that should all start with the same fields and share a `describe()` method. What role can a `BookRecord` class serve?

options.label: It stores every book as JSON text before any object can exist
It defines how new book instances are initialized and what shared methods they provide
It forces every book instance to contain identical field values
It replaces the need to call `new` when creating an instance

questions.explanation: A class defines the constructor and methods used by its instances. Constructor arguments can give each book different values; JSON conversion is separate, and the taught creation form uses `new`.

questions.prompt: Given `class BookRecord { constructor(title) { this.title = title; } }`, which expression creates an instance whose title is `"Orbit"`?

options.label: `BookRecord.title("Orbit")`
`class BookRecord("Orbit")`
`new BookRecord("Orbit")`
`constructor BookRecord = "Orbit"`

questions.explanation: `new BookRecord("Orbit")` creates an instance and passes the argument to its constructor. The other expressions do not use the taught JavaScript class-instantiation syntax.

questions.prompt: Inside a `BookRecord` instance method, what does `this.title` refer to?

options.label: The `title` property of the particular instance receiving the method call
A variable named `title` shared automatically by every JavaScript file
The text of the class name followed by the text of the method name
The first property of whichever object was created most recently

questions.explanation: For the taught instance-method call, `this` is the receiving instance, so `this.title` reads that instance’s property. It is not a global variable or a most-recent-object shortcut.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a JavaScript object from JSON in this week’s program?

options.label: They are interchangeable names for the same in-memory value
JSON can contain methods, while JavaScript objects cannot
A JavaScript object must be saved in a file before its properties can be read
The object is a JavaScript value in memory; JSON is text that can represent supported data

questions.explanation: A JavaScript object is a live language value. `JSON.stringify` can encode supported data as text, and `JSON.parse` can decode valid JSON text. JSON does not preserve methods as executable behavior.

questions.prompt: Which of these strings is valid JSON for one book record?

options.label: `{ title: "Orbit", returned: false }`
`{"title":"Harbor","returned":true}`
`{"title":"Atlas","returned":false,}`
`{"title":"Dawn","returned":undefined}`

questions.explanation: Valid JSON uses double-quoted property names and string values, allows the literal `false`, and has no trailing comma. Unquoted keys, `undefined`, and trailing commas are not valid JSON syntax.

questions.prompt: After `const text = JSON.stringify({ title: "Orbit", returned: false });`, what kind of value is `text`?

options.label: A string containing JSON text
A `BookRecord` class instance
An array containing two property names
A Boolean reporting whether conversion succeeded

questions.explanation: `JSON.stringify` returns a string representation of supported data. It does not construct a class instance, extract keys into an array, or return a success flag.

questions.prompt: What does this code print? `const book = { title: "Orbit", returned: false }; const text = JSON.stringify(book); book.returned = true; const copy = JSON.parse(text); console.log(copy.returned);`

options.label: `true`, because `copy` always tracks later changes to `book`
`undefined`, because parsed JSON has no properties
`false`, because `text` captured the earlier data and parsing creates a separate value
A syntax error, because JSON text cannot contain a Boolean

questions.explanation: Stringifying captures the supported values at that moment, including `returned: false`. Updating the original object does not rewrite the string; parsing that unchanged text creates a separate object whose property is still false.

skillCheck.title: Modules, Files, Tests, and Debugging Skill Check
skillCheck.instructions: Answer all 10 questions from the bounded Study resources and your own traces. You need 7/10 to pass. Options are reshuffled on every attempt, and attempts are unlimited.

questions.prompt: A Node project has `"type": "module"` in package.json. Which pair correctly shares the named `addTask` function from `tasks.js` with `cli.js`?

options.label: `tasks.js`: `export default addTask`; `cli.js`: `const { addTask } = require("./tasks")`
`tasks.js`: `module.exports = addTask`; `cli.js`: `import { addTask } from "tasks"`
`tasks.js`: `export function addTask() {}`; `cli.js`: `import addTask from "./tasks"`
`tasks.js`: `export function addTask() {}`; `cli.js`: `import { addTask } from "./tasks.js"`

questions.explanation: A named export is imported with matching braces. In Node ESM, a local relative import begins with `./` and includes the `.js` extension; the other pairs mix module systems, omit the relative path, or treat a named export as a default export.

questions.prompt: A project uses `import { addTask } from "./tasks.js"` in a `.js` file, but its package.json does not enable ECMAScript modules. Which project-level change matches the taught Node setup?

options.label: Add `"type": "module"` as a top-level field in package.json.
Rename the imported function to `module` without changing package.json.
Remove the relative `./` prefix so Node treats the file as ESM.
Put the import statement inside a JSON string in package.json.

questions.explanation: For this course's `.js` files, the taught Node ESM setup is a top-level `"type": "module"` field in package.json. Renaming a function, changing a relative specifier into a package specifier, or storing code as JSON text does not enable ESM.

questions.prompt: The file `data/tasks.json` contains a JSON array. Which expression reads it as text and produces the corresponding JavaScript array?

options.label: `JSON.stringify(readFileSync("data/tasks.json"))`
`JSON.parse(readFileSync("data/tasks.json", "utf8"))`
`readFileSync(JSON.parse("data/tasks.json"), "utf8")`
`writeFileSync("data/tasks.json", JSON.parse("utf8"))`

questions.explanation: `readFileSync` with `utf8` returns the file contents as text, and `JSON.parse` converts valid JSON text into JavaScript data. `JSON.stringify` moves in the opposite direction, while `writeFileSync` writes rather than reads.

questions.prompt: A loader currently catches every read or parse error and returns an empty array. If `tasks.json` exists but contains malformed JSON, what behavior protects the learner's saved records?

options.label: Report the malformed data and leave the existing file unchanged; create an empty collection only when the file is genuinely missing.
Treat every error as a new empty collection and save that collection over the existing file.
Delete the final character from the file repeatedly until `JSON.parse` accepts it.
Write an empty array before each read so the program always starts from valid JSON.

questions.explanation: A missing first-use file and a damaged existing file are different cases. Initializing only the missing file is safe; a parse failure should be visible and must not trigger a write that destroys the original evidence or records.

questions.prompt: A command changes one task and then saves the collection. Which order prevents an invalid read or failed update from overwriting the data file?

options.label: Write the current array, read it back, apply the update, and parse the returned value.
Create an empty file, apply the update, stringify the old array, and replace the empty file.
Stringify the command text, write it, parse the old file, and then attempt the update.
Read and parse, validate and apply the update, stringify the resulting collection, then write only after those steps succeed.

questions.explanation: The program should not write until it has successfully loaded valid data and produced a valid updated collection. Serializing and writing last keeps earlier failures from replacing the saved file with empty, old, or command-text data.

questions.prompt: A `node:test` case expects `findTasks(tasks, "review")` to return one task, but the assertion reports an empty array. What is the most useful interpretation of that failure?

options.label: The test runner has proved that every part of the application is broken.
The observed result differs from the stated expectation, so inspect both the search rule and the test data before deciding which one is wrong.
The expected value should always be replaced with the actual value so the test becomes green.
The failure can be ignored because only syntax errors reveal real defects.

questions.explanation: A failed assertion is specific evidence of an expected-versus-actual mismatch. It does not identify the cause by itself, so the next step is to inspect the function, inputs, and expectation rather than automatically changing the code or the test.

questions.prompt: `completeTask(tasks, 99)` must throw `RangeError("Task 99 was not found.")` without changing any task. Which test most directly checks the complete contract?

options.label: Complete the first existing ID and check only that its `completed` value becomes `true`.
Call the unknown ID inside a named function and assert only that some error is thrown.
Keep a copy of the fixture, assert that the named call throws the exact RangeError name and message, then deep-compare the original tasks with the copy.
Catch and ignore the error, then check only that the tasks array still has the same length.

questions.explanation: The supplied contract has three observable parts: the error class, its exact message, and unchanged input. `assert.throws` with the validation object checks the first two, while a deep comparison checks the third.

questions.prompt: For `node src/cli.js add "Blue backpack" "Main library" "Bag"`, which expression reads the command name `"add"` from Node's argument array?

options.label: `process.argv[2]`
`process.argv[0]`
`process.argv[1]`
`process.argv.slice(3)[0]`

questions.explanation: Node places the executable path at index 0 and the script path at index 1, so the first learner-supplied argument is at index 2. Slicing from index 3 would skip the command and begin with the description.

questions.prompt: Node provides `[nodePath, scriptPath, "add", "Blue backpack", "Main library", "Bag"]`. Which code reads the command and all three item fields?

options.label: `const args = process.argv.slice(1); const command = args[0]; const description = args[1]; const location = args[2]; const category = args[3];`
`const args = process.argv.slice(2); const command = args[0]; const description = args[1]; const location = args[2]; const category = args[3];`
`const args = process.argv[2].split(" "); const command = args[0]; const description = args[1]; const location = args[2]; const category = args[3];`
`const command = process.argv[0]; const description = process.argv[1]; const location = process.argv[2]; const category = process.argv[3];`

questions.explanation: `slice(2)` removes the Node executable and script paths, leaving the command at index 0 and its three quoted values at indexes 1, 2, and 3. Starting at index 1 keeps the script path; splitting only index 2 sees only `add`; direct low indexes read runtime paths.

questions.prompt: FoundIt is ready locally and contains no sensitive files. Which sequence follows the taught first-publication workflow for an existing project?

options.label: Push the folder first, then initialize Git and create a commit on GitHub.
Create a remote, delete the local project, then reconstruct it from the empty remote.
Commit only `data/items.json`, push it, and add source files in a later unrelated repository.
Initialize Git, inspect and stage the intended files, commit them, add the verified remote, then push the current branch.

questions.explanation: The taught existing-project route creates and reviews the local history before connecting the verified remote and pushing. Pushing before a local repository exists, deleting the project, or publishing only learner data does not produce the reviewed source repository.

questions.prompt: The `claim` command receives an existing item ID. Which sequence preserves the storage contract if validation or the claim rule fails?

options.label: Save an empty array, load the old records, mark every record claimed, then print the requested ID.
Parse the ID as JSON, write the command arguments, then load records to confirm the write.
Load valid records, validate the requested ID, apply the claim to the matching item, then save only the successful result.
Write the loaded records first, apply the claim afterward, and rely on the next command to save it.

questions.explanation: Loading and validation must succeed before a state-changing operation is saved. Applying the claim to the matching record and writing only the successful result prevents invalid input or failed lookup from replacing good data.

questions.prompt: Time permits four focused checks before FoundIt is submitted. Which set samples the most distinct required risks?

options.label: Add and list a valid item; search a known term; reject a missing claim ID; refuse malformed stored JSON without overwriting it.
Add four valid items with different descriptions and confirm that each success message appears.
Run the same successful add-list sequence four times against copies of one valid data file.
List seeded data, search a known term, claim a known ID, and list again, all using valid input.

questions.explanation: The first set spans a normal persisted flow, search behavior, an invalid identifier, and damaged storage. The other sets repeat happy-path behavior and leave either validation or storage failure unexamined.

Paste the full contents of every source file below the sentence.
State the Node prerequisite, exact run and test commands, command examples, data behavior, and known limits.
Replace the sentence with a list of commit dates and the author's weekly study hours.

questions.explanation: A useful handoff tells a new reader what is required and gives exact commands and examples, including how tests and saved data behave. Screenshots, copied source, or history do not replace executable setup and usage instructions.

questions.prompt: Before the first `git add`, the project folder contains `.env` with a token and `data/items.json` with personal test records. What is the safe next step?

options.label: Commit both files privately first, then delete them in a later public commit.
Move the token file out of the project, replace personal records with `[]` or a sanitized sample, then inspect every path before committing.
Rename `.env` to `token.txt` and keep the personal records because neither file contains JavaScript.
Push the folder, use the GitHub page to delete the files, and leave the earlier commit unchanged.

questions.prompt: FoundIt is committed locally, but the new commit does not appear on the GitHub repository page. Which check-and-action pair addresses the local-to-remote gap?

options.label: Run the CLI again, then refresh GitHub without using Git.
Run `git init` again inside `src`, then copy the output into the README.
Edit a second README on GitHub and assume it now contains the local source commit.
Verify the configured remote and current branch, push that branch, then confirm the commit on GitHub.

questions.explanation: A commit records work in the local repository; it does not transfer the commit to GitHub. Checking the remote and branch before pushing confirms the destination, and the repository page then verifies that the intended commit arrived.

questions.prompt: Which responsibility split makes FoundIt's search and claim rules testable without writing to the real data file?

options.label: `cli.js` owns every rule and file operation; `items.js` prints help; `storage.js` parses commands.
`storage.js` chooses commands; `items.js` prints results; `cli.js` edits JSON text directly.

Each module loads and saves its own copy of the records before returning a value.

templates.content:
# Record
{ id: number, description: string, location: string, category: string, status: "open" | "claimed" }
- First ID: 1; later ID: highest existing numeric ID + 1.
- Status values: "open" and "claimed" only.
- Display line: #1 [OPEN] Blue backpack | Main library | Bag

# Commands
node src/cli.js add "Blue backpack" "Main library" "Bag"
  -> Added item #1.
node src/cli.js list
  -> one display line per item, or: No items found.
node src/cli.js search "blue"
  -> case-insensitive substring match across description, location, and category; same display format, or: No items found.
node src/cli.js claim 1
  -> Claimed item #1.
node src/cli.js help
  -> print the Usage block below.

# Exact domain errors (CLI prefixes each with ERROR: )
add blank field -> TypeError("add requires non-blank description, location, and category.")
search blank text -> TypeError("search requires non-blank text.")
unknown item -> RangeError(`item #${id} was not found.`)
claimed item -> Error(`item #${id} is already claimed.`)
invalid claim text -> "claim requires a positive whole-number ID."
unknown command -> `unknown command "${command}".`
- Unknown or incomplete command usage prints its error, then help, and never saves.

# Usage
Usage:
  node src/cli.js add "<description>" "<location>" "<category>"
  node src/cli.js list
  node src/cli.js search "<text>"
  node src/cli.js claim <id>
  node src/cli.js help

questions.prompt: Nia wants to run the same welcome message tomorrow without retyping its JavaScript. Which approach best fits that goal?

questions.prompt: Omar changes the greeting in `hello.js`, but rerunning the file still shows the old greeting. What should he check first?

options.label: Whether the terminal text was selected before the command ran
Whether the JavaScript file was renamed after the first run
Whether the Node REPL contains a copy of the new greeting
Whether `hello.js` was saved before he reran the Node command

questions.explanation: Node reads the saved contents of the source file when the command runs. An unsaved editor change is not yet part of the file that Node executes.

questions.prompt: PowerShell is at `C:\Users\Maya`, while `hello.js` is inside `C:\Users\Maya\week-01`. Which command sequence runs that file from its folder?

options.label: `cd ./week-01` followed by `node ./hello.js`

`cd ./hello.js` followed by `node ./week-01`
`node cd ./week-01` followed by `./hello.js`

questions.explanation: `cd ./week-01` changes the current folder to the one containing the source file. From there, `node ./hello.js` asks Node to execute that file.

questions.prompt: A learner runs `node hello.js` and sees `Cannot find module C:\Users\Tara\hello.js`. VS Code shows the file at `C:\Users\Tara\practice\hello.js`. What does the error most strongly indicate?

questions.explanation: The path in the error shows exactly where Node looked. Because the real file is one folder deeper, the learner should enter `practice` or supply the correct path before rerunning the command.

options.label: VS Code is the runtime, and Node is the project folder

questions.explanation: `console.log(...)` sends its argument to the terminal output. A string expression by itself is not printed when it appears in a script run by Node.
